claim: Chronic antigenic stimulation can trigger the formation of interleukin 10 (IL-10)-producing T-regulatory type 1 (TR1) cells in vivo.
source: Chronic antigenic stimulation can trigger the formation of interleukin 10 (IL-10)-producing T-regulatory type 1 (TR1) cells in vivo.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that establishes a known biological phenomenon.

claim: Murine T-follicular helper (TFH) cells are precursors of TR1 cells.
source: We have recently shown that murine T-follicular helper (TFH) cells are precursors of TR1 cells
evidence: This claim is supported by previous work by the authors as indicated by 'recently shown'.

claim: The TFH-to-TR1 cell transdifferentiation process is characterized by the progressive loss and acquisition of opposing transcription factor gene expression programs.
source: the TFH-to-TR1 cell transdifferentiation process is characterized by the progressive loss and acquisition of opposing transcription factor gene expression programs that evolve through at least one transitional cell stage.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from recent work by the authors.

claim: The TFH-to-TR1 cell transition involves downregulation of TFH cell-specific gene expression due to loss of chromatin accessibility.
source: At the single-cell level, the TFH-to-TR1 cell transition is accompanied by both, downregulation of TFH cell-specific gene expression due to loss of chromatin accessibility
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell transcriptional and epigenetic data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The TFH-to-TR1 cell transition involves upregulation of TR1 cell-specific genes linked to chromatin regions that remain accessible throughout the transdifferentiation process.
source: upregulation of TR1 cell-specific genes linked to chromatin regions that remain accessible throughout the transdifferentiation process, with minimal generation of new open chromatin regions.
evidence: This is supported by the epigenetic analyses showing chromatin accessibility patterns.

claim: Most TR1-associated genes, including Il10, are already poised for expression at the TFH cell stage.
source: By interrogating the epigenetic status of accessible TR1 genes on purified TFH and conventional T-cells, we find that most of these genes, including Il10, are already poised for expression at the TFH cell stage.
evidence: This is supported by epigenetic analyses of TFH cells showing poised chromatin states.

claim: TR1-associated genes are closed and hypermethylated in Tconv cells.
source: Whereas these genes are closed and hypermethylated in Tconv cells
evidence: This is supported by methylation and chromatin accessibility data comparing Tconv cells to TFH and TR1 cells.

claim: TR1-associated genes are accessible, hypomethylated, and enriched for H3K27ac-marked and hypomethylated active enhancers in TFH cells.
source: they are accessible, hypomethylated, and enriched for H3K27ac-marked and hypomethylated active enhancers in TFH cells.
evidence: This is supported by ChIPseq, ATACseq, and methylation data from TFH cells.

claim: Active enhancers in TFH cells are enriched for binding sites for the TFH and TR1-associated transcription factors TOX-2, IRF4, and c-MAF.
source: These enhancers are enriched for binding sites for the TFH and TR1-associated transcription factors TOX-2, IRF4, and c-MAF.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of ChIPseq data for these transcription factors overlapping with active enhancers.

claim: The TR1 gene expression program is genetically imprinted at the TFH cell stage.
source: Together, these data suggest that the TR1 gene expression program is genetically imprinted at the TFH cell stage.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the epigenetic data showing that TR1 genes are already epigenetically marked in TFH cells.

claim: Systemic delivery of nanoparticles coated with peptide-major histocompatibility complex class II (pMHCII) molecules triggers the expansion and re-programming of cognate splenic T-follicular helper (TFH) CD4+ T-cells into TR1 cells.
source: We have shown that systemic delivery of nanoparticles (NPs) coated with mono-specific peptide-major histocompatibility complex class II (pMHCII) molecules (Singha et al., 2017) triggers the expansion and re-programming of cognate splenic T-follicular helper (TFH) CD4+ T-cells into expanded pools of transitional (referred to as TR1.1 or TR1-like) and terminally differentiated TR1 cells (referred to as TR1.2 or TR1)
evidence: This is supported by previous work cited (Singha et al., 2017).

claim: pMHCII-NP-induced TR1 cells resolve inflammation in various organ-specific autoimmune disease models in a disease-specific manner without impairing normal immunity.
source: that resolve inflammation in various organ-specific autoimmune disease models in a disease-specific manner without impairing normal immunity (Clemente-Casares et al., 2016; Umeshappa et al., 2020; Umeshappa et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by previous studies cited.

claim: pMHCII-NP therapy results from the sustained assembly of large TCR microclusters, and rapid, robust, and prolonged TCR signaling on TFH cells.
source: These events result from the sustained assembly of large TCR microclusters, and rapid, robust, and prolonged TCR signaling on TFH cells (Singha et al., 2017; Solé et al., 2023b; Solé et al., 2023a).
evidence: This is supported by previous studies cited.

claim: The antigen-specific TFH and TR1 sub-pools arising in response to pMHCII-NP therapy have nearly identical clonotypic composition but alternative functional properties and transcription factor (TF) expression profiles.
source: The antigen-specific TFH and TR1 sub-pools arising in response to pMHCII-NP therapy have nearly identical clonotypic composition but alternative functional properties and transcription factor (TF) expression profiles (Solé et al., 2023b).
evidence: This is supported by previous work cited (Solé et al., 2023b).

claim: pMHCII-NPs trigger cognate TR1 cell formation in TFH cell-transfused immunodeficient hosts.
source: In addition, pMHCII-NPs trigger cognate TR1 cell formation in TFH cell-transfused immunodeficient hosts
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous work.

claim: T-cell-specific deletion of Bcl6 or Irf4 blunts both pMHCII-NP-induced TFH expansion and TR1 formation.
source: and T-cell-specific deletion of two master regulators of TFH cell genesis (Bcl6 or Irf4) blunt both pMHCII-NP-induced TFH expansion and TR1 formation.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous work.

claim: Deletion of Prdm1 selectively abrogates the TFH-to-TR1 conversion.
source: In contrast, deletion of Prdm1 selectively abrogates the TFH-to-TR1 conversion.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous work.

claim: TFH cells can differentiate into TR1 cells in vivo.
source: Together, these data indicated that TFH cells can differentiate into TR1 cells in vivo
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cited studies.

claim: Blimp-1 is a gatekeeper of the TFH-to-TR1 cell re-programming event.
source: and that Blimp-1 is a gatekeeper of this cell re-programming event (Solé et al., 2023b).
evidence: This is a conclusion from previous work cited.

claim: pMHCII-NP-induced conversion of TFH cells into TR1 cells involves epigenetic re-programming of the TFH precursors.
source: The work described herein was initiated to test the hypothesis that pMHCII-NP-induced conversion of TFH cells into TR1 cells involves epigenetic re-programming of the TFH precursors.
evidence: This is stated as the hypothesis being tested in the current study.

claim: Chromatin modifications contribute to T-cell differentiation, such as during Th1/Th2 cell specification.
source: Although such processes have been shown to contribute to T-cell differentiation, such as during Th1/Th2 cell specification (O'Garra and Arai, 2000)
evidence: This is supported by a cited reference.

claim: Chromatin modifications can occur upon T-cell activation.
source: they can also occur upon T-cell activation (Avni et al., 2002)
evidence: This is supported by a cited reference.

claim: Chromatin modifications can occur in response to environmental cues, such as cytokine stimulation.
source: or in response to environmental cues, such as cytokine stimulation (Ostuni et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a cited reference.

claim: DNA methylation, histone modifications, and chromatin accessibility regulate T-cell activation and effector and memory responses during immune responses to infection.
source: Likewise, it has been established that DNA methylation, histone modifications, and chromatin accessibility regulate T-cell activation and effector and memory responses during immune responses to infection.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Effector T-cell-specific genes are demethylated and gain chromatin accessibility during T-cell differentiation.
source: Effector T-cell-specific genes are demethylated and gain chromatin accessibility and naïve T-cell-associated genes are repressed.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Naïve T-cell-associated genes required for survival are demethylated when effector cells become memory cells.
source: When these cells need to become memory, the naïve genes required for survival are demethylated (Belk et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a cited reference.

claim: In exhausted T-cells, numerous effector genes, such as Ifng, become closed, and acquire open chromatin at genes that are upregulated in these cells, such as Pdcd1.
source: Another notable example of chromatin remodeling is in exhausted T-cells, where numerous effector genes, such as Ifng, become closed, and acquire open chromatin at genes that are upregulated in these cells, such as Pdcd1 (Belk et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a cited reference.

claim: Th1 differentiation results in H3K4 di-methylation and H3 and H4 acetylation and in the creation of chromatin accessible regions at regulatory elements within the Ifng locus.
source: For example, Th1 differentiation results in H3K4 di-methylation and H3 and H4 acetylation and in the creation of chromatin accessible regions at regulatory elements within the Ifng locus, as well as in the loss of H3K27me3 through the locus (in addition to DNA demethylation of the locus) (Hatton et al., 2006; Schoenborn et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: Activation of the Th2 program leads to the loss of permissive histone modifications in Ifng, addition of repressive H3K27me3 marks along the locus and DNA methylation.
source: In contrast, activation of the Th2 program leads to the loss of permissive histone modifications in Ifng, addition of repressive H3K27me3 marks along the locus and DNA methylation (Schoenborn et al., 2007; Jones and Chen, 2006; Chang and Aune, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: Th2 differentiation from naïve precursors involves the acquisition of permissive histone modifications in Il4, Il5, Il13 and the locus control region (LCR), and the loss of H3K27me3 marks.
source: Th2 differentiation from naïve precursors also involves the acquisition of permissive histone modifications in Il4, Il5, Il13 and the locus control region (LCR), and the loss of H3K27me3 marks (Avni et al., 2002; Koyanagi et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: The promoters and eight gene regulatory elements (GREs) of Il17a and Il17f genes in naïve CD4+ T-cells acquire H3K27ac marks upon culture in Th17-polarizing conditions.
source: Likewise, the promoters and eight gene regulatory elements (GREs) of Il17a and Il17f genes in naïve CD4+ T-cells acquire H3K27ac marks upon culture in Th17-polarizing conditions (Akimzhanov et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a cited reference.

claim: Memory T-cells retain the positive histone modifications on their proximal and distal GREs that were acquired during differentiation of their precursor T-cells.
source: In memory T-cells, which display faster and greater levels of gene transcription than their naïve and effector counterparts, lineage-specific cytokine genes retain the positive histone modifications on their proximal and distal GREs that were acquired during differentiation of their precursor T-cells (e.g. H3K27ac and H3K9ac marks), even when expression of the genes ceases upon memory cell conversion, allowing rapid reactivation of these loci upon antigen re-encounter (Fann et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a cited reference.

claim: Naive CD8+ T cells lose repressive H3K27me3 marks during the primary immune response against infections, allowing rapid upregulation of Ifng and Gzmb expression by their memory CD8+ T-cell counterparts.
source: Likewise, naive CD8+ T cells lose repressive H3K27me3 marks during the primary immune response against infections, allowing rapid upregulation of Ifng and Gzmb expression by their memory CD8+ T-cell counterparts (Araki et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a cited reference.

claim: Memory T-cells retain the epigenetic signatures of their effector progenitors.
source: Overall, memory T-cells appear to retain the epigenetic signatures of their effector progenitors, thus allowing a quicker and more efficient response in subsequent antigen encounters.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cited studies.

claim: The Cd4 locus is hypermethylated in CD4–CD8–, CD4+CD8+ thymocytes and mature CD8+ T cells, but is demethylated in CD4+CD8–cells.
source: For example, the Cd4 locus is hypermethylated in CD4–CD8–, CD4+CD8+ thymocytes and mature CD8+ T cells, but is demethylated in CD4+CD8–cells (Teghanemt et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a cited reference.

claim: In naïve T-cells, Il4, Il5, Il13, and the corresponding LCR are hypermethylated and Ifng is hypomethylated.
source: Likewise, in naïve T-cells, Il4, Il5, Il13, and the corresponding LCR are hypermethylated and Ifng is hypomethylated (Fields et al., 2004; Lee et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: The methylation pattern of Il4, Il5, Il13, Ifng and the LCR is maintained during the Th0-Th1 differentiation process.
source: Whereas this methylation pattern is maintained during the Th0-Th1 differentiation process
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: During Th2 formation, Ifng becomes hypermethylated, and Il4, Il5, Il13, and the LCR demethylate key GREs.
source: it undergoes dramatic changes during Th2 formation, such that Ifng becomes hypermethylated, and Il4, Il5, Il13, and the LCR demethylate key GREs (Fields et al., 2004; Lee et al., 2002; Kim et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: TFH formation from naïve T-cell precursors involves demethylation of BCL-6 binding sites.
source: Likewise, TFH formation from naïve T-cell precursors involves demethylation of BCL-6 binding sites (Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a cited reference.

claim: In Foxp3+ Tregs, the expression of Foxp3 and genes coding for some Treg-function-associated molecules, such as Ctla4 and Il2ra, are associated with DNA demethylation.
source: In Foxp3+ Tregs, the expression of Foxp3 and genes coding for some Treg-function-associated molecules, such as Ctla4 and Il2ra, but not genes coding for TFs controlling other cell fates or cytokine genes that are repressed in Foxp3+ Tregs, are also associated with DNA demethylation (Liu et al., 2010; Ohkura et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: The development of memory T-cells involves progressive demethylation of promoter-distal GREs of key genes.
source: The development of memory T-cells also involves progressive demethylation of promoter-distal GREs of key genes (Durek et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a cited reference.

claim: Acquisition of new functional states by peripheral T-cells involves extensive and diverse modifications of the chromatin around specific loci.
source: Collectively, the above observations indicate that, in most cases, acquisition of new functional states by peripheral T-cells, including their differentiation into different T-cell subsets, involves extensive and diverse modifications of the chromatin around specific loci
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cited literature.

claim: The TFH-to-TR1 transdifferentiation process is associated with extensive contraction of the chromatin.
source: and that the TFH-to-TR1 transdifferentiation process is associated with extensive contraction of the chromatin
evidence: This is a main finding of the current study supported by the data presented.

claim: The TFH-to-TR1 transdifferentiation process involves upregulation of genes that are already epigenetically poised for expression at the TFH cell stage, such as Il10.
source: and the upregulation of genes that are already epigenetically poised for expression, yet are silent, at the TFH cell stage, such as Il10.
evidence: This is a main finding of the current study supported by the data presented.

claim: Genes upregulated during TFH-to-TR1 transdifferentiation are closed and hypermethylated in Tconv cells.
source: These genes are closed and hypermethylated in Tconv cells
evidence: This is supported by methylation and chromatin accessibility data.

claim: Genes upregulated during TFH-to-TR1 transdifferentiation are accessible, hypomethylated, and enriched for H3K27ac-marked and hypomethylated active enhancers in TFH cells.
source: but are accessible, hypomethylated, and enriched for H3K27ac-marked and hypomethylated active enhancers in TFH cells.
evidence: This is supported by ChIPseq, ATACseq, and methylation data.

claim: Genomic imprinting is a key enabler of the TFH-TR1 cell transdifferentiation process.
source: These data suggest that genomic imprinting is a key enabler of the TFH-TR1 cell transdifferentiation process, as documented in non-immune cell types (Holliday and Pugh, 1975; Muramoto et al., 2010; Raas et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data and supported by references to genomic imprinting in other cell types.

claim: BDC2.5mi/I-Ag7-specific CD4+ T-cells comprise a population of autoreactive T-cells that contribute to the progression of spontaneous autoimmune diabetes in NOD mice.
source: BDC2.5mi/I-Ag7-specific CD4+ T-cells comprise a population of autoreactive T-cells that contribute to the progression of spontaneous autoimmune diabetes in NOD mice.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about this T-cell specificity.

claim: Treatment with cognate pMHCII-NPs leads to the expansion and formation of anti-diabetogenic TR1 cells that retain the antigenic specificity of their precursors.
source: but treatment with cognate pMHCII-NPs leads to the expansion and formation of anti-diabetogenic TR1 cells that retain the antigenic specificity of their precursors (Clemente-Casares et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a cited reference.

claim: Treatment of hyperglycemic NOD mice with BDC2.5mi/I-Ag7-NPs results in the reversal of type 1 diabetes.
source: As a result, treatment of hyperglycemic NOD mice with these compounds results in the reversal of type 1 diabetes (Clemente-Casares et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a cited reference.

claim: The pMHCII-NP-induced Tet+ cell pools contain TFH and TR1 sub-pools (~30% and 70%, respectively).
source: Since the pMHCII-NP-induced Tet+ cell pools contain TFH and TR1 sub-pools (~30% and 70%, respectively) (Solé et al., 2023b; Solé et al., 2023a)
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: Cell clustering using the pMHCII-NP-induced Tet+ cell pool's two-dimensional scRNAseq and scATACseq dataset analysis revealed the presence of a well-defined TFH-like cell cluster and a larger cluster of cells containing both TR1-like and TR1 cells.
source: Cell clustering using the pMHCII-NP-induced Tet+ cell pool's two-dimensional scRNAseq and scATACseq dataset analysis using weighted nearest neighbor (WNN) revealed the presence of a well-defined TFH-like cell cluster and a larger cluster of cells containing both TR1-like and TR1 cells (Solé et al., 2023b).
evidence: This is supported by a cited reference and the data presented in Figure 1A.

claim: The KLH-induced TFH subset contained three sub-pools of TFH cells referred to as TFH.1, TFH.2, and TFH.3.
source: The KLH-induced TFH subset contained three sub-pools of TFH cells that we referred to as TFH.1, TFH.2, and TFH.3 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the scMultiome data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The scMultiome profile of the BDC2.5mi/I-Ag7-NP-induced TFH cell sub-pool overlapped with the KLH-induced TFH1.1 sub-pool, corresponding to effector Bcl6hiTox2hiIl21+Pdcd1+TFH cells.
source: The scMultiome profile of the BDC2.5mi/I-Ag7-NP-induced TFH cell sub-pool overlapped with the KLH-induced TFH1.1 sub-pool, corresponding to effector Bcl6hiTox2hiIl21+Pdcd1+TFH cells (Figure 1A, left).
evidence: This is supported by the scMultiome data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The KLH-induced TFH.2 cells expressed lower levels of Pdcd1, Il21, Bcl6, and Tox2 and higher levels of Maf, Tcf7, Cxcr5, and Cd69 compared to TFH.1 cells.
source: At the scRNAseq level, the KLH-induced TFH.2 cells were also similar to their TFH.1 counterparts but expressed lower levels of Pdcd1, Il21, Bcl6, and Tox2 and higher levels of Maf, Tcf7, Cxcr5, and Cd69 (Solé et al., 2023b).
evidence: This is supported by a cited reference.

claim: The KLH-induced TFH.3 cells display transcriptomic features of follicular T-regulatory cells (Foxp3+Bcl6+Bhlhe40+Icos+Il10+).
source: In contrast, the KLH-induced TFH.3 cells display transcriptomic features of follicular T-regulatory cells (Foxp3+Bcl6+Bhlhe40+Icos+Il10+) (Solé et al., 2023b).
evidence: This is supported by a cited reference.

claim: The BDC2.5mi/I-Ag7-NP-induced TFH cells and the KLH-induced TFH.1/TFH.2 cells were more similar to each other than to other cell subsets within each sample.
source: The transcriptional and epigenetic relationships among these various T-cell subsets were confirmed by hierarchical clustering of the two-dimensional scMultiome datasets (Figure 1B); despite coming from different mice and arising in response to different cues, the BDC2.5mi/I-Ag7-NP-induced TFH cells and the KLH-induced TFH.1/TFH.2 cells were more similar to each other than to other cell subsets within each sample.
evidence: This is supported by the hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: TFH cells undergo massive closure of OCRs as they transdifferentiate into TR1-like and TR1 cells.
source: Comparison of the scATACseq profiles of the KLH-induced TFH and BDC2.5mi/I-Ag7-NP-induced Tet+ TFH sub-pools indicated that TFH cells undergo massive closure of OCRs as they transdifferentiate into TR1-like and TR1 cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by the scATACseq data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Most of the OCRs that remain open in the terminally differentiated TR1 subset and the transitional TR1-like cells were already open at the TFH.1 cell stage.
source: The data further indicated that most, albeit not all, of the OCRs that remain open in the terminally differentiated TR1 subset and, especially, the transitional TR1-like cells were already open at the TFH.1 cell stage (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by the scATACseq data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The TFH-to-TR1 cell conversion process involves massive contraction of the chromatin and limited generation of new OCRs.
source: Thus, the TFH-to-TR1 cell conversion process involves massive contraction of the chromatin and limited generation of new OCRs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the scATACseq data.

claim: There were 2086 genes that were differentially expressed in TR1 vs. TFH cells.
source: Specifically, there were 2086 genes that were differentially expressed in TR1 vs. TFH cells.
evidence: This is supported by the scRNAseq data from the scMultiome dataset.

claim: Among the 2086 differentially expressed genes in TR1 vs. TFH cells, 1820 (87.2%) were downregulated and only 266 (12.8%) were upregulated.
source: Among these 2086 genes, 1820 (87.2%) were downregulated (e.g. Cxcr5, Il4, Bcl6, Nfia, Stat4, Tcf7, and Tox2) and only 266 (12.8%) were upregulated (e.g. Bach2, Cd226, Ccr5, Ifng, Il10, Lef1, Prdm1, and Tbx21) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by the scRNAseq data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: 94% (n=217/231) of the genes associated with chromatin regions that had closed during the TFH-TR1 conversion were downregulated.
source: Specifically, 94% (n=217/231) of the genes associated with chromatin regions that had closed during the TFH-TR1 conversion, but only 31% (n=4/13) of the newly acquired OCRs, were downregulated (the remaining 69% were upregulated) (p=8.25e-14) (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by the scMultiome data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Massive chromatin closure during the TFH-to-TR1 conversion is accompanied by significant gene downregulation.
source: Thus, massive chromatin closure during the TFH-to-TR1 conversion is accompanied by significant gene downregulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the scMultiome data.

claim: The relative frequency of upregulated and downregulated genes among those linked to the 1245 regions equally accessible in TR1 and TFH cells (n=196) was similar to that seen for global gene expression changes during the TFH-to-TR1 conversion (86.7% genes downregulated) (p=0.92).
source: In contrast, the relative frequency of upregulated and downregulated genes among those linked to the 1245 regions equally accessible in TR1 and TFH cells (n=196) was similar to that seen for global gene expression changes during the TFH-to-TR1 conversion (86.7% genes downregulated) (p=0.92) (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by the scMultiome data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Differential expression of genes linked to regions equally accessible in TR1 and TFH cells is likely regulated by factors other than chromatin exposure, such as TF availability, histone modifications, or DNA methylation.
source: Differential expression of these genes is thus likely regulated by factors other than chromatin exposure, such as TF availability, histone modifications, or DNA methylation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that chromatin accessibility does not correlate with differential expression for these genes.

claim: The TFH-to-TR1 cell conversion involves extensive remodeling of the chromatin and massive silencing of TFH gene expression.
source: Collectively, the above data indicate that the TFH-to-TR1 cell conversion involves extensive remodeling of the chromatin and massive silencing of TFH gene expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the scMultiome data.

claim: KLH-induced TFH cells contained 13 times more differential OCRs (as compared to Tconv cells) than their BDC2.5mi/I-Ag7-NP-induced Tet+ counterparts (n=10,919 vs. 821, respectively).
source: KLH-induced TFH cells contained 13 times more differential OCRs (as compared to Tconv cells; n=3) than their BDC2.5mi/I-Ag7-NP-induced Tet+ counterparts (n=10,919 vs. 821, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by bulk ATACseq data.

claim: 97.9% of the chromatin regions that are differentially exposed in pMHCII-NP-induced Tet+ cells (as compared to Tconv controls) are also differentially exposed in KLH-induced TFH cells.
source: Furthermore, the overwhelming majority of the chromatin regions that are differentially exposed in pMHCII-NP-induced Tet+ cells (as compared to Tconv controls) (97.9%) are also differentially exposed in KLH-induced TFH cells (Figure 2A and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by bulk ATACseq data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The chromatin regions that are differentially open in the pMHCII-NP-induced Tet+ and/or KLH-induced TFH cell pools (as compared to Tconv cells) are significantly associated with gene upregulation (p<7.88e-11).
source: In addition, the chromatin regions that are differentially open in the pMHCII-NP-induced Tet+ and/or KLH-induced TFH cell pools (as compared to Tconv cells, where these OCRs are closed) are significantly associated with gene upregulation (p<7.88e-11); no such association is found for genes linked to closed chromatin in either pMHCII-NP-induced Tet+ or KLH-induced TFH cells (p=0.86) (Figure 2B and Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by bulk ATACseq and RNAseq data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Chromatin closure in BDC2.5mi/I-Ag7-NP-induced Tet+ cells relative to KLH-induced TFH cells was associated with downregulation of gene expression.
source: Moreover, chromatin closure in BDC2.5mi/I-Ag7-NP-induced Tet+ cells relative to KLH-induced TFH cells was associated with downregulation of gene expression: 158 of the 341 genes that were downregulated in the former were linked to differentially closed OCRs (46.3%), as opposed to 94 of the 367 genes that were upregulated (25.6%) (p=1.38e-08) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by bulk ATACseq and RNAseq data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Studies of pMHCII-NP-induced Tet+ and KLH-induced TFH cells at the bulk level faithfully replicate the observations made using scMultiome.
source: Thus, studies of pMHCII-NP-induced Tet+ and KLH-induced TFH cells at the bulk level faithfully replicate the observations made using scMultiome.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing bulk and single-cell data.

claim: The TR1-like/TR1 cells contained within the Tet+ pool close a significant fraction of the chromatin as they transdifferentiate from TFH cells, leading to downregulation of gene expression.
source: Together, they indicate that the TR1-like/TR1 cells contained within the Tet+ pool close a significant fraction of the chromatin as they transdifferentiate from TFH cells, leading to downregulation of gene expression
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the bulk and single-cell ATACseq and RNAseq data.

claim: The chromatin that remains open in TR1 cells is already exposed at the TFH cell stage.
source: but the chromatin that remains open in TR1 cells is already exposed at the TFH cell stage.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the bulk and single-cell ATACseq data.

claim: The KLH-induced TFH, pMHCII-NP-induced Tet+, and the Tconv subsets had a similar number of H3K4me3 marked regions/peaks.
source: The KLH-induced TFH, pMHCII-NP-induced Tet+, and the Tconv subsets had a similar number of H3K4me3 marked regions/peaks (as defined via ChIPseq) (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by ChIPseq data.

claim: Most H3K4me3 marks (78%) were found at TSSs.
source: As expected, most of these H3K4me3 marks (78%) were found at TSSs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by ChIPseq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The overall H3K4me3 deposition landscape in BDC2.5mi/I-Ag7-NP-induced Tet+ cells is closer to that seen in KLH-induced TFH cells than in their Tconv counterparts.
source: The heatmaps shown in Figure 3A (left) show that the overall H3K4me3 deposition landscape in BDC2.5mi/I-Ag7-NP-induced Tet+ cells (containing ~70% TR1 cells) is closer to that seen in KLH-induced TFH cells than in their Tconv counterparts (at the global level, including all chromatin regions, both open and closed at the TR1 cell stage) (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by ChIPseq data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: There were only 123 differentially marked H3K4me3 peaks between Tet+ and TFH cells (adjusted p<0.01).
source: There were only 123 differentially marked H3K4me3 peaks between Tet+ and TFH cells (adjusted p<0.01)
evidence: This is supported by ChIPseq data.

claim: Most of the differentially marked H3K4me3 peaks between Tet+ and TFH cells were linked to areas of the chromatin that were closed in TR1 cells as compared to their TFH precursors, except for two genes (Ptpn11 and Angptl2).
